topic: how solar panels turn sunlight into electricity
why: Following light from a garden lamp to a rooftop helps your child explain a hidden cause with pictures and words.
teaser: Shade a garden light and it glows, then follow tiny packets of light as they knock electrons down a one-way slide.
title: How Solar Panels Turn Sunlight into Electricity
question: How can a dark square of glass turn sunlight into electricity?
idea: A solar cell is a thin slice of silicon made in two layers. Where the layers meet, a built-in push acts like a one-way slide. Light knocks electrons loose, and the push sends them round a wire. One cell gives only a small push, so panels join many cells in a row.

curiosity.intro: Start with a garden light that glows when you shade it. Then follow sand to a cell, peek inside, count the cells in a panel, and visit a snowy roof.
curiosity.carryForward: Next time you pass a solar panel, look for its rows of cells and thin silver lines.

questions.question: Why is a solar cell dark blue?
questions.notice: Follow the row from sand to a grey lump, a shiny slice and a dark blue cell.
questions.say: A solar cell is made of silicon, which is made from sand. Bare silicon is shiny, and it bounces away about a third of the light that hits it. Makers add a coat thinner than a soap bubble. The coat makes the cell look dark blue and helps it keep more light.
questions.try: Look at a shiny spoon and a dark mug in sunlight. Which one throws more glare into your eyes? Shiny things keep less light.

questions.question: How does light make electricity?
questions.notice: Find the two thin layers and the tiny beads near the line where they meet.
questions.say: Light travels in tiny packets called photons. A photon with enough energy can knock an electron loose inside the silicon. Where the two layers meet, a built-in push acts like a one-way slide. It sends loose electrons out through a wire, round the loop and back in the other side. That flow is electricity.
questions.try: Stand in a circle with your family and hold hands. Pass a gentle squeeze all the way round. Electrons move round a loop of wire in a similar way.

questions.question: Why does a panel need so many cells?
questions.notice: Count the cells in one row and find the thin silver lines on each cell.
questions.say: One silicon cell gives a push of only about half a volt. A small battery gives about three times that. So makers join cells end to end, and the small pushes add up. Many panels hold 36 cells or more. The thin silver lines are wires that gather the electrons.
questions.try: Stack three books. Each one is a small step, but together they make a tall one. Cells add their pushes the same way.

questions.question: Why do panels like cold, bright days?
questions.notice: Find the snow on the roof and the clear, dark panels in the low light.
questions.say: Heat makes everything inside the silicon jiggle more, and that weakens the push of each cell. In the same sunshine, a cold panel makes more power than a hot one. Most of the sunlight that lands on a panel turns into heat, not electricity.
questions.try: Lay a dark cloth and a white cloth in the sun for ten minutes. Which one feels warmer? Dark panels warm up in the sun, too.

reading.title: The dark square on the garden light

beats.title: A light that waits
beats.passage: Little Wonderer finds a garden light on the path. On its cap is a small dark square with thin silver lines. The little one holds a mitten over the square. Click! The tiny lamp glows, as if night came early. Big Wonderer leans in to look. How can a small square tell day from night?

foldable.heading: A light that waits

beats.title: From sand to cell
beats.passage: That dark square is a solar cell, and it starts as sand. Sand holds silicon, a shiny grey stuff. Workers melt it, grow a big crystal, and slice it thinner than a fingernail. Bare silicon is so shiny that it bounces sunlight away. A thin coat turns it dark blue, so more light soaks in.
beats.prompt: Why does the cell get a thin blue coat?

foldable.heading: From sand to cell
foldable.body: A solar cell starts as sand. Silicon is melted, sliced thin and given a blue coat so it keeps more light.

beats.title: A one-way slide
beats.passage: Sunlight comes in tiny packets called photons. Inside the cell, two thin layers are pressed together. Where they meet, there is a push that works like a one-way slide. A photon knocks a tiny electron loose. The slide sends it out one side, along a wire and through the lamp. Then it comes back in the other side. That flow is electricity.
beats.prompt: What does a photon do inside the cell?

foldable.heading: A one-way slide
foldable.body: Light comes in tiny packets called photons. Each can knock an electron loose. A one-way slide sends it round a wire.

beats.title: Cells in a row
beats.passage: Here is a clue. A big panel is made of many small cells in rows. One cell gives only a small push, about half a volt. A small battery gives about three times as much. So the cells are joined end to end, and their pushes add up. Thin silver lines on each cell gather the electrons.
beats.prompt: Why are so many cells joined in a row?

foldable.heading: Cells in a row
foldable.body: One cell gives only a small push. A panel joins many cells in rows, so all their small pushes add up.

beats.title: Shade means night
beats.passage: Back on the path, Big Wonderer holds a leaf over the garden light. The little one points as the lamp glows again. Now the guess changes. The square does not keep sunlight like a sponge. It pushes electrons only while light lands on it. All day, that push fills a little battery inside. When shade stops the push, the light thinks it is night.
beats.prompt: Why does the lamp glow in the shade?

foldable.heading: Shade means night
foldable.body: The square pushes only while light lands on it. When shade stops the push, the garden light thinks it is night.

beats.title: Cold and bright
beats.passage: Here is a surprise. Solar panels like cold, bright days. Heat makes the inside of each cell jiggle, so its push gets weaker. In the same sunshine, a cold panel makes more power than a hot one. In 1954, one of the first useful silicon panels spun a toy Ferris wheel. How could a panel stay cool in the sun?
beats.prompt: Why does heat weaken a solar panel?

foldable.heading: Cold and bright
foldable.body: Heat weakens the push of each cell. In the same sunshine, a cold panel makes more power. How could it stay cool?

math.title: Sunlight story numbers
math.intro: Six one-step stories about garden lights, cells, panels and sunny roofs. Add or subtract to find each answer.

tasks.label: TASK 1
tasks.prompt: Little Wonderer counts 27 garden lights on one path and 18 on another. How many garden lights is that altogether?
tasks.hint: Add the ones, then the tens. Trade 10 ones for 1 ten if needed.
tasks.worked: 27 + 18 = 45. Combine the lights on both paths.

tasks.label: TASK 2
tasks.prompt: A box holds 64 thin silicon slices, and 29 of them are made into cells. How many slices are still plain?
tasks.hint: Trade 1 ten for 10 ones if needed, then subtract the ones and tens.
tasks.worked: 64 − 29 = 35. Take away the slices that became cells.

tasks.label: TASK 3
tasks.prompt: In a pretend count, 36 photons knock electrons loose, and then 47 more do. How many electrons are knocked loose in all?
tasks.hint: Add the ones, then the tens. Trade 10 ones for 1 ten if needed.
tasks.worked: 36 + 47 = 83. Combine both groups of loose electrons.

tasks.label: TASK 4
tasks.prompt: A panel has 60 cells, and a tree shades 24 of them. How many cells are still in the sun?
tasks.hint: Trade 1 ten for 10 ones if needed, then subtract the ones and tens.

tasks.label: TASK 5
tasks.prompt: Big Wonderer counts 45 minutes of sun on the garden light in the morning and 37 in the afternoon. How many minutes is that altogether?
tasks.hint: Add the ones, then the tens. Trade 10 ones for 1 ten if needed.
tasks.worked: 45 + 37 = 82. Combine the morning and afternoon minutes.

tasks.label: TASK 6
tasks.prompt: A snowy town has 72 roof panels, and snow still covers 35 of them. How many panels are clear?
tasks.hint: Trade 1 ten for 10 ones if needed, then subtract the ones and tens.
tasks.worked: 72 − 35 = 37. Take away the panels under snow.

math.extension: After you finish, tell which problem felt most like a sunny roof, and why.

beats.passage: That dark square is a solar cell, and it begins as ordinary sand, which holds a shiny grey material called silicon. Workers melt the silicon, grow it into a big crystal, and slice it into wafers thinner than a fingernail. Bare silicon is so shiny that it bounces away about a third of the light that hits it. beats.passage: Sunlight arrives in tiny packets of energy called photons. When a photon with enough energy knocks an electron loose, the slide sends it out one side of the cell, along a wire, through the lamp and back in the other side. Light with too little energy cannot free an electron. Extra energy simply warms the cell.

beats.passage: Here is a clue that makes the idea easier to trust. A big panel is a grid of many small cells, joined in long rows by thin silver ribbons. poem.title: The Coolest Panel
lines: Little Wonderer found a flat square of blue
with silver-thin stripes running all the way through.
“It’s sleeping,” the little one whispered. “Don’t peep.”
“It’s working,” said Big Wonderer. “Too bright to sleep.”
“The sunshine comes down in small packets of light.
Each knocks an electron loose, left and right.
A one-way slide inside sends it off down the wire,
round the lamp and back home, and it never gets tired.”
“A hot panel,” the big one said, “loses its push.
It works best when it’s cool.” And then, with a whoosh,
the little one hurried away down the hall
to make it the hardest-working panel of all.
It’s frosty in there, and it’s cool as can be,
tucked in with the ice cubes and bags of green peas.
The coldest, best panel that ever was found,
but it’s dark when that door shuts. Not one spark goes round.
